questions.stem: When comparing two datasets, you should always make statements about:

options.text: Both an average and a measure of spread
Only the mean
The number of data items
Only the range

questions.explanation: A complete comparison requires both an average (to compare typical values) and a measure of spread (to compare consistency).

questions.stem: Class A has mean 65 and range 40. Class B has mean 58 and range 12. Which class is more consistent?

options.text: Class A, because the range is larger
They are equally consistent
Class B, because the range is smaller
Class A, because the mean is higher

questions.explanation: A smaller range indicates less spread and more consistency. Class B's range of 12 is much smaller than Class A's range of 40.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Team X is better because their range is higher.' What is wrong with this statement?

options.text: The student should have used the mode instead
The range should be compared with the median, not used alone
Nothing is wrong -- a higher range is always better
A higher range means more spread, which usually means less consistency, not better performance

questions.explanation: A higher range means scores are more spread out, indicating less consistency. This is typically not 'better' -- it means performance is unpredictable.

questions.stem: Why is it unfair to compare the mean of one dataset with the median of another?

options.text: Because the mean is always larger
Because different averages measure different things
It is perfectly fine to do this
Because medians only work for small datasets

questions.explanation: The mean and median measure the 'centre' of data differently. The mean is affected by outliers while the median is not, so comparing them directly is not a fair comparison.

questions.stem: Two factories produce bolts. Factory A: mean diameter 10.0 mm, range 0.3 mm. Factory B: mean diameter 10.2 mm, range 1.5 mm. Which factory should you choose for reliable manufacturing?

options.text: Either factory -- the results are the same
Factory A, because the range shows it is much more consistent
Factory B, because the range is larger
Factory B, because the mean is closer to the target

questions.explanation: Factory A has a much smaller range (0.3 mm vs 1.5 mm), meaning its bolts are far more consistent. For reliable manufacturing, consistency is crucial.

questions.stem: For skewed data, the best measures to use for comparison are:

options.text: Mean and range
Median and interquartile range
Mean and standard deviation
Mode and range

questions.explanation: The median and IQR are resistant to extreme values and skew, making them the most appropriate measures for comparing skewed distributions.

questions.stem: When writing a comparison, you should always:

options.text: Use technical language without context
Quote the actual values and relate them to the context of the question
Draw a chart before making any comparison
Only state which dataset is 'better'

questions.explanation: A good comparison quotes actual values (e.g. 'mean of 62 vs 58') and relates them to context (e.g. 'Class A scored higher on average in the maths test').
